The parable that made him a household name has him handing each of his three sons a single arrow to snap easily, then a bundle of three to show it could not be broken: stay united and the Mōri are unbreakable. (Historians doubt the scene ever happened, but the message — bind your heirs together — was real enough that he placed sons into neighboring clans to control them.) He warned his family against overreach, and they survived by it long after flashier dynasties were gone.

events.label: Date Masamune, the one-eyed dragon
events.description: The fierce, flamboyant "one-eyed dragon" of the far northeast, who carved out a great domain late in the game — too late to win Japan, but bold enough to send his own embassy across two oceans.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Childhood smallpox cost him his right eye, hence the nickname; legend says he gouged out the dangling eye himself. Born a generation too late to contend for the country, he submitted to Hideyoshi and then Ieyasu and channeled his ambition into spectacle and a flair for the dramatic — he and his swaggering retainers are often credited as the origin of the word date-otoko, a 'dandy' or stylish man. Most remarkably, in 1613 he built a Western-style galleon and dispatched a samurai, Hasekura Tsunenaga, on a years-long embassy across the Pacific to Mexico, then on to Spain and Rome to meet the Pope — one of the first Japanese missions to cross the ocean to Europe and back.

events.label: Portuguese arrive at Tanegashima with guns
events.description: A storm drives a Chinese junk carrying two Portuguese adventurers onto the southern island of Tanegashima — and the matchlock muskets aboard change Japanese warfare forever.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The island's young lord, Tanegashima Tokitaka, bought two of the guns and set his own smiths to reverse-engineering them. The famous sticking point was the screw that plugged the barrel's base — a fastener Japan didn't yet use — and tradition says a smith only cracked it by marrying his daughter to a Portuguese gunner to learn the secret. Within a decade Japanese smiths were mass-producing 'tanegashima,' and the weapon spread like wildfire through the warring domains. In a striking reversal, Japan would within a few generations become one of the most heavily gun-armed nations on earth — then, under the peace, deliberately set the technology aside.

events.label: Francis Xavier brings Christianity
events.description: The Jesuit Francis Xavier lands at Kagoshima and opens the Christian mission to Japan — a faith that took root fast, drawing hundreds of thousands of converts, some lords among them, before the backlash.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Xavier was startled by the Japanese, calling them the best people his order had yet found among 'the heathen,' and he wrestled hard with how to translate Christian ideas into a Buddhist vocabulary — an early attempt to render 'God' borrowed a Buddhist word and badly confused his listeners. The mission's shrewdest move was top-down: convert a daimyō and his whole domain often followed, which is how the faith spread so fast. Some lords converted from genuine belief, others to secure the lucrative Portuguese trade that traveled with the missionaries. That entanglement of God and guns and silver was exactly what later made the unifiers suspect the Christians of being a foreign fifth column — and turn on them savagely.

events.label: The Nanban ("southern barbarian") trade
events.description: Portuguese ships from Macau bring silk, guns, and curiosities to Japan in exchange for its silver, opening a vivid age of European contact the Japanese painted in gold on folding screens.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Nanban means 'southern barbarians' — the Europeans arrived from the south, via Macau and Goa, and the name stuck. The traffic was really a clever triangle: the Portuguese, allowed into China when Japan was not, ferried Chinese silk to silver-rich Japan and Japanese silver back to China, pocketing the spread. The contact poured exotica into Japan — tobacco, bread (the Japanese word pan still comes from Portuguese), eyeglasses, clocks, Western painting — and Japanese artists captured the big-nosed visitors, their billowing pantaloons, and their black ships in a whole genre of brilliant nanban folding screens. It was Japan's first sustained look at Europe, and Europe's first real look at Japan.

events.label: Oda Nobunaga begins his rise
events.description: A wild, brilliant young lord of a minor Owari domain inherits his father's lands — written off as a fool, the "Great Fool of Owari," he would become the most disruptive man of the age.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His youth was so erratic — odd dress, rough company, public misbehavior — that one of his father's old retainers reportedly killed himself in protest to shock the heir into seriousness, a death that may have genuinely jolted him. What looked like folly was partly a different mind: Nobunaga had no use for pedigree or tradition where results were concerned. He grasped earlier than his rivals what the Portuguese matchlock could do, embraced commerce and 'free markets' to fund his wars, and promoted men by talent alone — most famously a sandal-bearer of peasant birth named Kinoshita, the future Toyotomi Hideyoshi. The fool was the one who saw the future coming.

events.label: Battle of Okehazama
events.description: Wildly outnumbered, Nobunaga gambles everything on a single lightning raid through a thunderstorm — and kills the mighty warlord Imagawa Yoshimoto, the upset that announced him to all Japan.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Imagawa Yoshimoto was marching on Kyoto with an army many times Nobunaga's size and had paused to rest in a narrow wooded gorge, celebrating early victories — overconfident, his troops scattered and at ease. Nobunaga, scorning a hopeless siege defense, slipped his small force around through cover and fell on the command camp just as a violent thunderstorm broke and masked his approach. Yoshimoto, the story goes, thought a drunken brawl had erupted among his own men before the enemy was upon him; he was cut down before he understood what was happening. One reckless strike erased a great rival and made the 'fool of Owari' suddenly a man to fear.

events.label: Nobunaga marches into Kyoto
events.description: Nobunaga marches into the capital escorting a claimant to the shogunate, installs him as a puppet, and seizes the political center of Japan — the reunification has begun.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He came under cover of legitimacy: Ashikaga Yoshiaki, brother of the murdered shogun Yoshinori's line, was desperate for a strongman to restore him, and Nobunaga supplied the army in exchange for control. Holding the capital and a tame shogun gave Nobunaga the priceless ability to issue commands in the shogun's name and brand his enemies rebels against the rightful order. His ambition was carved on a famous seal he began using around this time — Tenka Fubu, 'the realm under one sword,' or all the land brought under military rule. It was less a slogan than a program: one man, by force, over the whole of Japan.

events.label: Nobunaga burns Mount Hiei
events.description: To smash a centuries-old religious power once and for all, Nobunaga sends his army up sacred Mount Hiei, burns the great Enryaku-ji monastery to the ground, and massacres everyone he finds.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Enryaku-ji had loomed over Kyoto for 800 years, a vast Tendai complex of thousands of buildings whose warrior-monks had bullied emperors and shoguns alike and were now sheltering Nobunaga's enemies. He treated the holy mountain as a military target: troops ringed it, set it ablaze, and cut down monks, women, and children together — contemporary accounts speak of thousands dead. It was an act of shocking sacrilege that horrified even hardened warriors, and it announced Nobunaga's iron rule that no power, not even the gods', stood above his. The breaking of armed Buddhism as a political force in Japan effectively begins on that burning mountain.

events.label: The last Ashikaga shogun expelled
events.description: The puppet shogun Yoshiaki schemes against his puppet-master; Nobunaga simply drives him out of Kyoto, and the 237-year Ashikaga shogunate quietly ends — not with a battle but an eviction.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Yoshiaki chafed at being a figurehead and secretly wove together an 'encirclement' of Nobunaga's enemies — the Takeda, the Asai and Asakura, the militant temples, even the distant warlords — hoping to bring his overmighty patron down. Nobunaga slipped the noose, beat the allies piecemeal, and in 1573 expelled Yoshiaki from the capital. Tellingly, he did not bother to kill him or take the shogun's title for himself; the office had become so hollow that ending it was an afterthought. The institution Yoritomo's invention had spawned, that had ruled or shadowed Japan for centuries, expired almost unnoticed — the future would belong to a new kind of overlord.

events.label: Battle of Nagashino
events.description: Nobunaga lines up ranks of matchlock gunners behind wooden palisades and shatters the famous Takeda cavalry charge — a battle long taught as the day massed guns ended the age of the mounted warrior.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The classic story is that Nobunaga fielded 3,000 gunners firing in three rotating ranks — one volley while two reload — to maintain a continuous wall of fire, and that the elite Takeda horsemen broke themselves against the palisades and the bullets. Modern historians have picked the legend apart: the neat three-rank rotation is probably a later embellishment, the gun count is disputed, and terrain, field fortifications, and sheer numbers mattered as much as the matchlocks. But the core is sound — disciplined massed firepower beat heavy cavalry decisively, the Takeda never recovered, and Nagashino became the symbol of the gun's arrival as the master weapon of Japanese war.

events.label: Azuchi Castle built
events.description: Nobunaga raises a dazzling seven-story tower-keep above Lake Biwa — less a fortress than a palace and a billboard, declaring a new age of monumental castles and one-man power.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Azuchi was a statement in architecture. Its great keep rose in seven gleaming stories with interiors blazing in gold leaf and walls painted by the master Kanō Eitoku, the top floors lacquered and gilded — built to overawe, not just to defend. Nobunaga, who recognized no power above himself, reportedly had a temple put there for visitors to venerate him, a gesture of near self-deification. The castle stood only a few years: in the chaos after Nobunaga's assassination in 1582 it burned and was abandoned, leaving little but its massive stone base. It survives as the template — the soaring decorative tenshu keep that every great castle after it, Osaka and Himeji included, would imitate.

events.label: The Ishiyama Hongan-ji war ends
events.description: After a grinding ten-year war, Nobunaga finally forces the surrender of the great fortified temple-fortress at Osaka, breaking the militant Pure Land leagues that had defied him longest.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ishiyama Hongan-ji was the headquarters of the Ikkō-ikki, a temple turned fortress so strong it took Nobunaga a full decade to reduce — his single most stubborn enemy. Its defenders, believing death in the holy war guaranteed them paradise, fought with a fearlessness that unnerved his troops, and the temple was repeatedly resupplied by sea by the Mōri fleet, which is why Nobunaga had to build armored warships to choke it off. It fell only when the emperor brokered a surrender in 1580. Its site was so commanding that Hideyoshi soon raised his colossal Osaka Castle on the very same ground — defeated faith's fortress becoming triumphant power's seat.

events.label: The Incident at Honnō-ji
events.description: On the brink of conquering all Japan, Nobunaga is betrayed by one of his own top generals, trapped in a Kyoto temple, and dies in the flames — the most shocking murder of the age, its motive still a mystery.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Nobunaga was resting at the temple of Honnō-ji with only a small guard when his general Akechi Mitsuhide — sent to reinforce another front — turned his army on the temple instead, reportedly declaring 'the enemy is at Honnō-ji.' Surrounded and wounded, Nobunaga set the temple ablaze and died inside; his body was never found, fueling centuries of speculation. Why Mitsuhide did it is one of Japanese history's great unsolved questions — grudge, ambition, fear, even conspiracy theories have all been argued. His triumph lasted barely twelve days: Hideyoshi raced back and destroyed him, which is why Mitsuhide is remembered by the bitter phrase 'a ruler of three days.'

events.label: Hideyoshi avenges Nobunaga at Yamazaki
events.description: Hearing of his master's murder, the peasant-born general Hideyoshi makes peace overnight, races his army back across Japan at astonishing speed, and crushes the traitor Mitsuhide within days.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Hideyoshi was besieging a castle far to the west when Nobunaga died. His genius was speed: he secretly cut a deal with the enemy he was fighting, then forced-marched his army back toward Kyoto with stunning urgency — the famous 'Great Return from Chūgoku,' roughly 125 miles in a handful of days, the kind of logistics most rivals couldn't imagine. He reached Yamazaki before the other generals had even gathered their wits and destroyed Mitsuhide's outnumbered force; Mitsuhide was killed fleeing, reportedly by peasant bandits. By avenging Nobunaga first, Hideyoshi claimed the moral right to inherit him — turning a foot soldier's son into the front-runner to rule Japan.

events.label: Toyotomi Hideyoshi takes power
events.description: The ultimate gekokujō story: a man born a peasant, with no clan, no name, and no land, out-maneuvers Nobunaga's heirs and rivals to become the most powerful man in all Japan.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: No one of his birth had ever come close to ruling Japan, and everyone knew it — Nobunaga is said to have nicknamed him 'monkey' (saru) for his looks. He outplayed the field after Nobunaga's death not mainly by battle but by politics: at a council to choose Nobunaga's successor he championed the murdered lord's infant grandson, making himself the child's 'protector' and thus the real power, then beat the rival generals who objected. Climbing required ever-grander names: the obscure foot soldier eventually had himself granted the entirely new surname 'Toyotomi' by the emperor. His own rise was living proof of the upside-down age — which is exactly why he then slammed the door shut behind him, freezing the social order so no one could repeat it.

events.label: Osaka Castle built
events.description: Hideyoshi raises the largest castle in Japan on the ruins of the temple-fortress Nobunaga spent a decade breaking — a colossal seat of national power, deliberately out-building even Azuchi.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He built it on the commanding site of Ishiyama Hongan-ji, the very stronghold that had defied Nobunaga for ten years — defeated faith's fortress becoming triumphant power's throne. Its scale and gold-leaf splendor were meant to broadcast that one man now ruled, and its walls were anchored by enormous quarried stones, some weighing well over a hundred tons, dragged to the site by tens of thousands of laborers. The castle's history mirrors its dynasty's fate: the Toyotomi heir would make his last stand here, and Tokugawa armies stormed and burned it in 1615. What towers over Osaka today is a 20th-century reconstruction on the old foundations.

events.label: Hideyoshi becomes imperial regent (kampaku)
events.description: Locked out of the shogun's title by his peasant birth, Hideyoshi takes a different and even higher road to legitimacy — having himself made kampaku, the emperor's chief regent.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: By tradition the title of shogun went to men of Minamoto descent, a bloodline a peasant could not fake. The office of kampaku, on the other hand, had for centuries belonged exclusively to the Fujiwara aristocracy — yet Hideyoshi maneuvered into it anyway, reportedly by exploiting a succession quarrel among the noble houses and getting himself adopted into the right family to qualify. Where a shogun ruled as the emperor's general, the kampaku ruled as the emperor's civil deputy, an even loftier perch. It was a dazzling piece of social climbing: the man with no pedigree had borrowed the highest dignity the ancient court could bestow, and ruled the country through the emperor's own authority.

events.label: Sen no Rikyū perfects the tea ceremony
events.description: Hideyoshi's tea master Sen no Rikyū carries the wabi tea ceremony to its severe perfection — turning the preparing and sharing of a bowl of tea into one of the supreme arts of Japanese culture.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His vision was radical reduction. He shrank the tea room to as little as two mats, lit it dimly, and fitted it with a doorway so low that even a great lord had to crawl in on his knees, swords left outside — making everyone equal and humble before the tea. He prized the plain, the rough, the cracked, and the worn over anything gold or imported, distilling the whole aesthetic into the idea of wabi-sabi, beauty in imperfection and impermanence. He codified principles still taught today — often summed up as harmony, respect, purity, and tranquility. The strange thing is the setting: this monk-like cult of simplicity flourished at the court of the gaudiest, most golden-castled ruler Japan had ever seen.

events.label: Hideyoshi's sword hunt
events.description: Hideyoshi orders every sword, spear, and gun stripped from the farmers, monks, and commoners — disarming the countryside that had risen in peasant leagues, and slicing the warrior off from everyone else.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: It was shrewdly sold as piety, not repression: the edict claimed the confiscated weapons would be melted down to make nails and bolts for a giant statue of the Buddha, so that surrendering your sword earned you merit in this life and the next. The real aim was control — to make the armed peasant uprisings and warrior-monk armies of the Sengoku impossible ever again. Coming from a man who had himself risen from peasant to ruler with a borrowed spear, it was the ladder being kicked away: never again would a commoner climb the way he had. Together with his land survey, it drew a hard, permanent line between the sword-bearing samurai and the disarmed farmer below.

events.label: The Taikō land survey
events.description: Hideyoshi has all of Japan measured field by field and rated by its rice yield in koku — the most thorough land survey in the country's history, and the spreadsheet on which the new order ran.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Surveyors fanned out across the realm with standardized measuring rods and a single fixed size for the unit of land area and the volume of a koku, replacing the chaos of local customs with one national accounting. Crucially, each plot was registered to one cultivator who owed the tax — which swept away the old shōen tangle of three or four overlapping claimants on a single paddy that had been the great legal headache of the medieval age. It pinned farmers to their land and fixed exactly what every domain was worth, so a lord could be assigned, taxed, or transferred by his precise kokudaka. With the survey and the sword hunt together, the fluid Sengoku world was being frozen into a measured, registered, immovable order.

events.label: Siege of Odawara and reunification
events.description: Hideyoshi besieges the last great holdout, the Hōjō fortress of Odawara — and wins it not by storming the walls but by laying siege with such overwhelming leisure that he reunifies Japan almost as theater.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Rather than batter the famously strong castle, Hideyoshi surrounded it with a vast army and simply settled in for months in luxurious comfort — bringing tea masters, courtesans, merchants, and entertainers, and even building a whole fortress, Ishigakiyama, in secret behind screens and then dramatically revealing it overnight to break Hōjō morale. The defenders, meanwhile, dithered through endless councils, giving rise to the Japanese phrase 'Odawara conference' for a meeting that talks forever and decides nothing. The Hōjō surrendered; their leaders were ordered to commit suicide. With the Kantō subdued, the whole of Japan answered to one man for the first time in over a century.

events.label: The class-separation edict
events.description: Hideyoshi makes it illegal to change your station — no samurai turning farmer, no farmer turning townsman or soldier — freezing the fluid Sengoku into the rigid class order the Tokugawa would inherit.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The aim was to lock down the very mobility that had defined the warring-states age, when a peasant could pick up a spear and rise — exactly Hideyoshi's own path. The decree separated the warrior from the farmer for good: samurai were pulled into the castle towns as a distinct ruling caste, while farmers were bound to the soil and forbidden to leave their fields. This hardened over time into the inherited four-tier scheme later summed up as 'shi-nō-kō-shō' — warrior, farmer, artisan, merchant — that would order Japanese society for nearly three centuries of Tokugawa peace. The man who climbed the ladder made sure to saw off every rung behind him.

events.label: Hideyoshi forces Sen no Rikyū to commit suicide
events.description: At the height of his fame, the great tea master is ordered by his own patron to disembowel himself — a chilling, still-unexplained turn that exposed the paranoia growing in the aging Hideyoshi.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The trigger most often cited is almost absurdly petty: a temple Rikyū had funded placed a wooden statue of him in its upper gateway, which meant Hideyoshi, passing beneath, would symbolically walk under the tea master's feet — taken as an unforgivable arrogance. But the real causes were surely deeper: a clash of wills between an autocrat who loved gold and a master who preached the plain, court intrigue, suspected disloyalty. Rikyū was allowed the dignity of seppuku rather than execution. He is said to have held a final tea gathering for his closest followers, given away his utensils, and then taken his own life — composing, by tradition, a defiant death verse as he went. Genius and absolute power could not, in the end, share a room.

events.label: First invasion of Korea (Imjin War)
events.description: His ambition swollen past Japan, Hideyoshi hurls a vast army at Korea as a stepping-stone to conquering Ming China itself — and the dream runs aground on Korean resistance and a brilliant admiral.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: On land the gun-armed, battle-hardened Japanese stormed up the peninsula and took the Korean capital within weeks. But at sea Korean admiral Yi Sun-sin annihilated Japanese fleets again and again, partly with armored 'turtle ships' — low, spike-roofed warships designed to ram and blast through enemy lines — choking off the supply lines the overstretched land armies depended on. Some historians read the whole adventure as Hideyoshi solving a domestic problem abroad: a way to spend the dangerous energies of an army of warriors he no longer needed at home, by pointing them at the mainland. It bled Japan for years and gained nothing — a conqueror's overreach that left only ruin on both shores.

events.label: Ming China intervenes in Korea
events.description: Ming China pours armies into Korea to defend its tributary — turning Hideyoshi's lunge at the mainland into a grinding three-way war that bleeds everyone and conquers nothing.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: For the Ming, this was non-negotiable: Korea was its loyal tributary and its buffer, and a Japanese army on the Korean border meant a Japanese army at China's doorstep, so the emperor sent tens of thousands of troops to throw it back. The combined Ming-Korean counterattack, plus Korean guerrillas and Yi Sun-sin's navy savaging the supply lines, drove the Japanese back toward the southern coast, where the war congealed into a stalemate. Years of inconclusive peace talks followed, sabotaged in part because Hideyoshi's demands — including a Ming princess as a bride — were so outrageous that his own envoys reportedly faked the negotiations to keep him from learning the truth. The talks collapsed, and the killing resumed.

events.label: The persecution of Christians begins
events.description: Suspicion of the foreign faith turns to blood: Hideyoshi has twenty-six Christians crucified at Nagasaki — the first martyrs of a persecution the Tokugawa would later carry to brutal extremes.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The twenty-six were a mix of foreign missionaries and Japanese converts, and chillingly, several were boys — the youngest only twelve or so. They were marched hundreds of miles in winter to Nagasaki, the heart of Japanese Christianity, and crucified on a hill there as a public warning. Behind the cruelty lay real fears: that the rapid spread of Christianity created a population loyal to a foreign pope and prince, and that the missionaries were the advance guard of European conquest, as had happened in the Philippines and the Americas. Hideyoshi's bans were fitful; under the Tokugawa the campaign would harden into a relentless, generations-long extermination of the faith.

events.label: Second invasion of Korea
events.description: When the peace talks collapse, Hideyoshi flings a second, even crueler army at Korea — and only his own death the next year ends the disaster, forcing a humiliating Japanese withdrawal.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The second campaign was markedly more brutal and quickly bogged down, never matching the first invasion's early sweep. Its most infamous legacy is the practice of cutting off the noses of the Korean dead and prisoners — and even civilians — pickling them in salt, and shipping them home as proof of kills for reward. They were buried in a mound in Kyoto grimly miscalled the 'Ear Mound' (Mimizuka), which still stands. When Hideyoshi died in 1598 the council of elders kept his death secret and quietly ordered the armies home. Six years of war had ravaged Korea, drained Japan, and gained absolutely nothing — a catastrophe born wholly of one dying man's overreach.

events.label: Death of Hideyoshi
events.description: The peasant who conquered Japan dies leaving only a five-year-old heir and a council of five great lords sworn to protect him — a child, a war abroad, and a power vacuum begging to be exploited.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He spent his last energy on a frail safeguard: the Council of Five Elders, the realm's most powerful lords, made to swear repeated oaths to defend little Hideyori until he came of age. The most powerful elder of all was Tokugawa Ieyasu — the obvious threat, bound by promises Hideyoshi surely doubted he would keep. Dying, the old conqueror reportedly begged the council again and again to protect his son, and is said to have left a death poem comparing his whole dazzling rise to a fleeting dream: 'like dew I fall, like dew I vanish... all of Osaka is a dream within a dream.' The war in Korea was hastily called off, and within two years his careful arrangements collapsed into the showdown at Sekigahara.

events.label: Tokugawa Ieyasu, the patient regent
events.description: The supreme art of waiting: Ieyasu had outlasted Nobunaga and served Hideyoshi for decades, biding his time — and now, with the master dead and the heir a child, the patient man's moment had come.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His patience was forged early and hard: as a boy he spent over a decade as a political hostage, a pawn traded between rival warlords, learning to survive by reading other men. A famous (later) verse contrasts the three unifiers by how each would handle a cuckoo that won't sing: Nobunaga would kill it, Hideyoshi would coax it to sing, and Ieyasu would simply wait until it sang — the proverbial summary of his whole character. He held the richest domain in Japan, the Kantō plain around Edo, and had carefully avoided spending his armies in the ruinous Korean war. Where Hideyoshi gambled and grasped, Ieyasu watched, endured, and let his rivals exhaust themselves — and then struck.

events.label: Battle of Sekigahara
events.description: Two vast coalitions, perhaps 160,000 men, collide in a fog-bound mountain valley to decide Japan — and a single mid-battle betrayal turns the day and the next two and a half centuries.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: For hours the morning fog and the savage fighting left the outcome genuinely in doubt; on paper, with reserves uncommitted, the western army may even have held the better position. The hinge was treachery already arranged in the dark: the young lord Kobayakawa Hideaki, holding a hill with a large force, had secretly promised Ieyasu he would switch sides. When he hesitated, Ieyasu — by the famous story — ordered his own gunners to fire on Kobayakawa's lines to force his hand. Kobayakawa charged downhill into his own allies, the western line buckled and collapsed, and by afternoon it was over. One man's broken oath made Ieyasu master of Japan.

events.label: William Adams, the English samurai
events.description: An English navigator washes ashore half-dead from a doomed Dutch voyage — and improbably becomes the trusted advisor and personal samurai of the future shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Adams arrived in 1600 aboard the Liefde, the last survivor of a Dutch expedition that set out with five ships and reached Japan a wreck crewed by dying men. The Portuguese Jesuits, fearing a Protestant rival, urged Ieyasu to execute him; instead Ieyasu was fascinated, kept him close as an interpreter and counselor on the wider world, had him build Western-style ships, and granted him a fief, swords, and samurai rank under the Japanese name Miura Anjin — 'the pilot of Miura.' Forbidden to leave, he lived out his life in Japan. His extraordinary story — the foreigner turned samurai — became the seed of James Clavell's novel and the hit series Shōgun.

events.label: Tokugawa Ieyasu becomes shogun
events.description: Ieyasu has the emperor name him shogun and founds the Tokugawa regime at Edo — reviving the ancient warrior title and beginning 250 years of peace and near-total isolation.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Unlike the peasant Hideyoshi, Ieyasu could claim — through a conveniently arranged genealogy — descent from the Minamoto, which qualified him for the shogun's title Hideyoshi could never hold. His shrewdest move came fast: after just two years he abdicated in favor of his son, while keeping real power as 'retired shogun,' to prove the office was now hereditary Tokugawa property and head off any succession crisis. He learned the deepest lesson of the whole medieval age — that the Minamoto and Ashikaga regimes both decayed and fell — and built his to last by locking down the daimyō, the foreigners, and the social order. It worked: the Tokugawa shogunate endured until 1868.

events.label: Himeji Castle and the great castle age
events.description: The dazzling white "White Heron" castle of Himeji rises in its great form — the supreme surviving example of the soaring Japanese castle that the unification age perfected and the peace then froze.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Its nickname, the White Heron, comes from the brilliant white fire-resistant plaster sheathing its walls and from a silhouette that seems poised to take flight. Behind the beauty is a war machine: the route to the central keep is a deliberate maze of curving paths, blind turns, gates, and dead ends meant to confuse and trap attackers under fire from above. It is the finest of the dozen-odd original keeps that survive — most Japanese castles were torn down under later policy, in war, or rebuilt in concrete — and almost miraculously came through both the great purges of castles and the bombing of World War II nearly untouched. Today it is a UNESCO World Heritage site and Japan's most visited castle.

events.label: Miyamoto Musashi and the duelist tradition
events.description: The age's most famous swordsman: a masterless wanderer who claimed some sixty undefeated duels and, in old age, set down his philosophy of combat in The Book of Five Rings.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Musashi developed a distinctive two-sword style, fighting with the long and short blades at once, and was famous for winning by psychology and improvisation as much as steel. His most legendary duel, against the master Sasaki Kojirō on a remote island, has him arriving deliberately late to rattle his opponent and striking the killing blow with a wooden sword he had carved from a spare oar on the boat over. Late in life he withdrew to a cave and wrote Go Rin no Sho, The Book of Five Rings — a treatise on strategy and the warrior mind still read today by martial artists and, famously, by business executives hunting for an edge. He is the human face of the rōnin, the masterless samurai the closing of the wars set adrift.

events.label: The katana and the sword-smith's art
events.description: Japan's smiths perfect the curved, folded-steel katana — a blade hard enough to hold a razor edge yet tough enough not to shatter, and the object that became inseparable from the samurai's soul.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The genius is a contradiction solved by craft. A smith folds and hammer-welds the steel many times to drive out impurities and build up layers, then wraps a soft, springy core in a harder skin. The signature curve and the wavy temper line (hamon) along the edge are born in the final quench: the spine is painted with thick clay and the edge with thin, so the edge cools fast and turns glass-hard while the spine cools slow and stays flexible — and the uneven shrinkage bends the blade into its curve. The result is a sword that takes a deadly edge without snapping. Revered smiths like Masamune of the Kamakura era became near-legends, their surviving blades treated as national treasures.

events.label: Samurai armor evolves for the gun age
events.description: Guns rewrote what armor had to do: out went the old laced-plate suits built to stop arrows, in came the solid-plate tōsei-gusoku, "modern armor" forged to turn a bullet — technology answering technology.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Older Japanese armor was made of hundreds of small scales laced together with silk cords — flexible and beautiful, but heavy when wet, slow to repair, and useless against a musket ball. The new style favored large solid iron plates, sometimes deliberately dented by a test shot (the tameshi mark) to prove they were bulletproof, and was faster and cheaper to mass-produce for armies now numbering in the tens of thousands. Some lords also imported European breastplates outright, the nanban-dō or 'southern-barbarian armor.' Freed from pure function, the helmets exploded into fantastic shapes — antlers, crescent moons, rabbit ears, sea creatures — as warlords competed to be unmistakable, and terrifying, on a smoke-filled battlefield.

events.label: Folding screens and the Kanō school
events.description: As the warlords built golden castles, the Kanō painters gave them golden art: bold, swaggering tigers, pines, and hawks splashed across gold-leaf walls and screens — the very opposite of austere Zen ink.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: This was art as power, made to glow in the dim interiors of a castle keep: huge motifs in heavy mineral pigments laid over solid gold-leaf grounds, so the surfaces shimmered in lamplight and dwarfed anyone standing before them. Its towering genius, Kanō Eitoku, decorated Nobunaga's Azuchi and Hideyoshi's castles, working (the sources say) on so vast a scale and to such relentless deadlines that he wore himself out and died young. The Kanō school made itself the indispensable painters of the powerful — and survived by it, serving as official artists to the rulers of Japan for the next three centuries, right through the Tokugawa age.

events.label: Raku tea bowls created
events.description: Working to Rikyū's taste, the potter Chōjirō makes tea bowls by hand instead of on the wheel — squat, irregular, low-fired raku ware, ceramics that wear their imperfection on purpose.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Raku bowls are shaped by hand and carving tool, never thrown on a wheel, then fired at low temperature and pulled glowing-hot straight from the kiln — a fast, rough process that yields thick, warm, slightly uneven bowls comfortable to cradle and slow to scald the lips. Their plain, dark, asymmetric look was the deliberate opposite of glossy, perfect Chinese porcelain, and exactly the humble wabi spirit Rikyū wanted. The name itself came from above: Hideyoshi granted the family a seal bearing the character 'raku' (ease, enjoyment), and Chōjirō's descendants still make raku ware in Kyoto today — an unbroken family line of more than four centuries.

events.label: Korean potters and the "pottery wars"
events.description: The Korean invasions came home with human plunder: kidnapped Korean potters who, forced to work for their captors, founded Japan's greatest ceramic traditions — culture seized at gunpoint.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The campaigns are sometimes bitterly nicknamed the 'pottery wars' (or 'teabowl wars') because Japan's tea-obsessed lords prized Korean ceramics so highly that capturing the potters who made them was a war aim in itself. The abducted craftsmen carried knowledge Japan lacked — and crucially, a Korean named Yi Sam-pyeong is credited with discovering the right porcelain clay near Arita around 1616, launching Japan's first true porcelain industry. Satsuma and Arita-Imari ware grew from these uprooted communities into world-famous traditions, later exported across Europe. It is one of history's grimmest ironies: a brutal failed conquest's most lasting fruit was a flowering of beauty, built on stolen lives and skills.

events.label: Movable-type printing arrives
events.description: Japan meets movable-type printing twice at once — from Jesuit missionaries and from the Korean war — enjoys a brief golden age of it, then quietly goes back to carving whole pages from wood.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Jesuits set up a European press that printed Christian texts and even Japanese classics in romanized script (the 'Kirishitan editions'), while the Korean campaign brought back captured Korean metal type and printing know-how; the imperial court and shogunate both produced fine movable-type books around 1600. Yet within a few decades it faded. Movable type suits an alphabet of a few dozen letters, but Japanese needs thousands of distinct characters and a flowing, cursive script that reads more naturally carved as continuous images — so for printing whole pages of beautiful Japanese, hand-cut woodblocks were simply better, and they won out. The technology that revolutionized Europe lost, on its merits, to the older Japanese way.

events.label: Christian daimyō and the Tenshō embassy
events.description: Three Christian lords send four Japanese boys on an astonishing journey — across two oceans to Lisbon, Madrid, and Rome to kneel before the Pope — the first Japanese embassy ever to reach Europe.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The four teenage envoys, of samurai families, were sent on a Jesuit initiative partly as living proof to European patrons that the Japan mission was worth funding. The round trip took about eight years; they were feted across Catholic Europe, met two popes, and dined with kings, a sensation on both sides. But they came home in 1590 to a country that had turned: Hideyoshi had begun moving against Christianity, and the faith they represented was sliding toward persecution. The journeys of these boys mark the high point of Japan's openness to Europe — after which the door began, slowly and then completely, to close on the world they had crossed oceans to see.

events.label: The Heike Monogatari and the war tales
events.description: Recited from memory by blind lute-priests, The Tale of the Heike turned the Genpei War into national poetry — and gave Japan its lasting image of the doomed, elegant samurai.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: For centuries it was less a book than a performance: itinerant blind monks called biwa hōshi chanted it to the plucked notes of the biwa, a kind of lute, and the written versions we have were stitched together from those sung recitations. Its famous opening — the sound of the temple bells, the truth that 'the proud do not endure, they are like a dream on a spring night' — frames the whole epic as a Buddhist sermon on impermanence, with the glittering Taira cast as the proud who must fall. That is exactly why historians read it warily: it invents speeches, sharpens heroes and villains, and bends messy events to fit a moral. Much of what 'everyone knows' about the samurai is really the Heike's literature, not the record.

events.label: Yoshida Kenkō's Tsurezuregusa
events.description: A monk jots down whatever drifts through his idle mind — and accidentally writes Essays in Idleness, the book that fixed the medieval Japanese taste for the imperfect and the impermanent.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Its very title and opening confess the method: 'with nothing better to do,' Kenkō says, he scribbles down the random thoughts that cross his mind 'all day long,' which is why the book wanders freely from sharp social observation to ghost stories to grumbling about etiquette. Its enduring core is a celebrated defense of imperfection: 'Are we to look at cherry blossoms only in full bloom, the moon only when cloudless?' — the falling petal and the veiled moon, he argues, move us more than perfection ever could, because their passing is the point. That single idea became a near-official statement of the Japanese aesthetic, and the book is still read in schools today — though, tellingly, it was largely ignored in its own century and only became a classic generations later.

events.label: The Kamakura new Buddhism reshapes faith
events.description: Pure Land, Zen, and Nichiren together tore Buddhism loose from the monasteries and handed it to ordinary people — the deepest religious change in Japanese history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The old Buddhism was effectively closed to commoners: to be saved you more or less had to be a monk with years of study, or rich enough to pay monks to perform rituals for you. The new movements blew that open by making the practice almost shockingly simple — chant a short formula, or just sit in meditation — so a farmer, a fisherman, or a dying old woman could do it with no literacy, no wealth, and no Sanskrit. What looks like a flowering of sects was really one radical idea taking several forms at once: that salvation belongs to everyone, not only to the learned and the rich. The schools founded in this single burst — Pure Land, True Pure Land, Rinzai and Sōtō Zen, Nichiren — remain the largest branches of Japanese Buddhism today.

events.label: The Mongol invasions and the seppuku ideal
events.description: Seppuku — ritual suicide by cutting open one's own belly — hardens during the medieval wars into a warrior's last assertion of will, defeat turned into a final proof of honor.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The belly was no accident: the Japanese located a person's spirit and true intent in the abdomen (hara), so opening it was a way of laying your sincerity bare for all to see. In its developed form the act was an excruciating, deliberate ordeal — a horizontal cut, sometimes a second vertical one — which is why a trusted second, the kaishakunin, eventually stood by to behead the dying man and cut short the agony. It began as a battlefield choice (mass suicides like the hundreds of Hōjō who disemboweled themselves when Kamakura fell in 1333) and only later, under the peace, became a formal, ceremonial, even judicial punishment — the honorable death sentence handed to a samurai instead of execution.

events.label: Ji-zamurai and the village warrior
events.description: Far below the famous warlords sat the ji-zamurai — local landholding fighters who plowed their own fields and took up arms when needed, the broad rural base of the whole warrior world.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: These were warrior and farmer in one person, living on and working the land they held rather than drawing a stipend in a castle town — the medieval norm, when the line between soldier and peasant was blurry and porous. As the natural leaders of their villages, ji-zamurai often headed the sworn ikki leagues that resisted tax collectors and warlords. That very independence made them a target of the unifiers' new order: Hideyoshi's sword hunt and his class-separation edicts forced exactly these men to choose — give up the sword and become full farmers bound to the soil, or give up the land and become full retainers in a lord's castle town. The amphibious village warrior was legislated out of existence.

events.label: The ashigaru foot soldier transforms armies
events.description: War stops being a contest of noble mounted archers and becomes a clash of massed infantry: the ashigaru, common foot soldiers in their thousands, become the force that actually decides battles.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The name means 'light feet.' They began as irregular, lightly-equipped recruits, often little better than looters — but Sengoku warlords drilled them into disciplined blocks wielding the cheap weapons of mass war: first long pikes (yari) packed shoulder to shoulder like a hedge, then, after the Portuguese guns arrived, ranks of matchlocks. A peasant could be trained to fire a matchlock in weeks, where a horse-archer took a lifetime — so a lord's strength came to be measured in how many foot soldiers he could field, not how many noble cavalry. It was a quiet social revolution: the battlefield, the very heart of samurai prestige, now belonged to the commoner with a gun.

events.label: The koku and the rice economy
events.description: Power in Japan came to be measured not in acres or gold but in rice: the koku, roughly the rice to feed one person for a year, became the yardstick of a lord's wealth, rank, and army size.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: A koku is about 5 bushels (180 liters) of rice. The logic was brutally practical — rice fed soldiers, so a domain's rice yield directly told you how big an army its lord could raise and feed; rough rules of thumb let a lord reckon how many warriors a given koku assessment owed for war. A domain's whole worth was stated as its kokudaka, its taxable rice output, and a daimyō was officially a lord of so many thousand koku. The system was so central that samurai stipends under the later peace were paid in koku of rice rather than coin, and the wealthiest domain, Kaga, was famously 'the million-koku domain' — Japan kept score in grain.

events.label: The ninja of Iga and Kōga
events.description: The real kernel behind the black-clad legend: families from the rugged Iga and Kōga districts who hired out as spies, scouts, saboteurs, and assassins in an age that prized such dirty work.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The historical shinobi were specialists in intelligence and irregular warfare, not the silent black-suited acrobats of film — that costume mostly comes from Edo-era theater, where stagehands dressed in black to be 'invisible,' an image later pinned onto the ninja. Iga and Kōga were poor, defensible mountain districts that governed themselves through leagues of small families and turned their survival skills into a marketable trade. Their autonomy ended violently: Oda Nobunaga, enraged by their resistance, invaded Iga in 1581 and slaughtered much of its population. Surviving Iga and Kōga men later served Tokugawa Ieyasu — by tradition, helping smuggle him to safety across the mountains after Nobunaga's assassination.

events.label: Kabuki's wild beginnings
events.description: A female shrine entertainer named Izumo no Okuni dances a flashy, risqué new spectacle on a dry Kyoto riverbed — and invents kabuki, exactly as the warring age yields to the Tokugawa peace.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The very word kabuki comes from kabuku, 'to lean' or 'to be outlandish' — slang for the gaudy, swaggering, rule-breaking style of the age's flashy youth, which Okuni mimicked on stage, a woman often dressed as a dandy man. It began as bawdy, sexy, popular entertainment, with troupes of women whose performances shaded into prostitution. The Tokugawa shogunate, obsessed with order, eventually banned women from the stage entirely — which is why all kabuki roles, female included, came to be played by men (the onnagata female-role specialists). The riverbank spectacle of 1603 grew into one of Japan's great classical theaters, born at the exact hinge between the medieval world and the long Edo peace.

events.label: Negoro and the warrior monks
events.description: For centuries Japan's great temples kept their own armies of warrior-monks who could march on the capital to bully the court — until the unifiers decided armed religion was just another rival to crush.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The sōhei were a power the kenmon system had lived with for ages: monasteries like Mount Hiei could send mobs of armed monks down on Kyoto to extort rulings, even carrying their shrine's sacred objects to make defying them a sin. The Negoro monks went further and embraced the new technology, becoming famous gunsmiths and crack matchlock troops. That made them too dangerous to tolerate. Nobunaga had already burned Mount Hiei; in 1585 Hideyoshi stormed and torched the Negoro temple complex, ending the warrior-monks' centuries of military independence. Religion was disarmed and folded under the warlord state — one more autonomous power the unifiers refused to leave standing.

events.label: Nagasaki opens as a Christian port
events.description: A Christian lord opens the deep-water harbor of Nagasaki to Portuguese ships, and a fishing village swells into Japan's great window on the world — and the beating heart of its Christianity.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Its convert lord, Ōmura Sumitada, took the extraordinary step of actually donating the town to the Jesuits in 1580, briefly making Nagasaki something close to a Church-run territory on Japanese soil — exactly the foreign-controlled enclave that alarmed Hideyoshi, who seized it back in 1587. The port's whole history then inverted. Once the country sealed itself off, Nagasaki became the single chink left in the wall: the lone harbor where, on the fan-shaped artificial islet of Dejima, a handful of Dutch and Chinese traders were permitted to do business under tight guard. The center of Japanese Christianity became the center of Japanese persecution, and the one tiny keyhole through which Japan and the West could still glimpse each other.

events.label: The Asakura and the fall of the old houses
events.description: Nobunaga wipes out venerable, deep-rooted clans like the Asakura and Asai — proof that in the Sengoku, centuries of pedigree counted for nothing against ability and pitiless force.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Asai betrayal nearly killed Nobunaga: his brother-in-law Asai Nagamasa turned on him mid-campaign in 1570, catching him between two armies, and he barely escaped. He spent three years grinding both houses down and finished them in 1573. His hatred ran cold and personal — by a notorious account he later had the lacquered, gilded skulls of the Asai and Asakura lords displayed at a New Year's banquet. The message of these extinctions was the dark twin of gekokujō: the same age that let nobodies rise also let ancient dynasties be erased overnight. Lineage was no longer protection, only a target, and a new ruling class would be built from scratch by the victors.

events.label: Tokugawa Ieyasu makes Edo his capital
events.description: Handed the Kantō as a half-trap by Hideyoshi, Ieyasu plants his base at the marshy village of Edo — the obscure backwater that would swell into Tokyo, the largest city on earth.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The move was partly a demotion in disguise: Hideyoshi pried Ieyasu loose from his ancestral home provinces and parked him in the distant, undeveloped east, hoping to weaken him. Ieyasu turned the exile into a foundation. Edo was a tiny castle town on a swampy bay; he and his heirs drained marshes, cut canals, diverted rivers, and built a sprawling castle and city around it. Under the later Tokugawa policy that forced every daimyō to keep a residence and family there, Edo mushroomed into one of the biggest cities in the world, passing a million people in the 1700s. Renamed Tokyo, 'eastern capital,' in 1868, the backwater Hideyoshi used as a dumping ground became the heart of modern Japan.

events.label: Ishida Mitsunari and the western alliance
events.description: Hideyoshi's brilliant but unloved administrator, Ishida Mitsunari, rallies the lords who feared and resented Ieyasu into the western coalition — and stakes the Toyotomi cause on the field of Sekigahara.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Mitsunari's tragedy was that he was a desk man in a world of warriors. A superb bureaucrat who had run Hideyoshi's surveys, logistics, and finances, he was widely disliked by the great battlefield generals as a meddling penpusher, which fatally weakened the loyalty of his own coalition. He fought to defend the boy Hideyori's inheritance against Ieyasu's encroachments, but when his allies wavered or defected at Sekigahara, his army collapsed. Captured days later, he was paraded and beheaded in Kyoto. By legend he faced death with composed dignity — even, the famous story goes, refusing a persimmon offered on the way to execution because it might upset his health, drawing a wry remark that a condemned man need not worry about his digestion.

events.label: Kobayakawa's battlefield defection
events.description: The man whose nerve decided an empire: at the crisis of Sekigahara the young lord Kobayakawa Hideaki turned his army on his own allies — the single act of treachery that shaped Japan's next 250 years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Hideaki was Hideyoshi's own nephew by marriage, which made his betrayal of the Toyotomi cause especially bitter. He had secretly agreed to defect to Ieyasu, but on the day he froze — torn, terrified, watching the battle hang in the balance from his hill — until Ieyasu's bullets snapped him into motion and he poured down onto the western flank. He got his reward in lands, but not peace: he died only about two years later, barely twenty-one, his early death and his torments widely read by contemporaries as a kind of judgment on the traitor. The most consequential decision of the battle was made by perhaps its least heroic figure.

events.label: The tea ceremony as politics
events.description: Hideyoshi turned tea into theater of power: a vast public tea festival at Kitano open to all, and a fully portable golden tea room — the austere ritual bent into a tool of dazzling political display.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The 1587 Grand Kitano gathering was a propaganda spectacle: Hideyoshi proclaimed it open to everyone from great lords to commoners, anyone who loved tea, even foreigners, told them to bring nothing fancier than a kettle and a mat, and displayed his own priceless tea treasures for the crowds — advertising himself as a ruler of refinement and largesse. His golden tea room was the opposite extreme of his master Rikyū's rustic ideal: collapsible walls, ceiling, and utensils all of gold, packable for travel so he could perform tea-as-power anywhere, even reportedly carrying it into the imperial palace. The same man patronized the cult of plainness and built a tea room of solid gold — tea served two opposite masters in his hands, beauty and propaganda.

events.label: The fall of the Takeda clan
events.description: The mighty house of Takeda Shingen, terror of the Sengoku, is hunted to extinction by Nobunaga and his allies — one of the age's great dynasties snuffed out in a matter of weeks.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Shingen's feared cavalry had been broken at Nagashino in 1575, and under his less able son Katsuyori the domain steadily crumbled. In 1582 a swift Oda-Tokugawa invasion shattered it as vassals defected en masse rather than die for a losing cause — a final demonstration of how fast loyalty evaporated when a lord's luck turned. Katsuyori, abandoned, killed his family and himself, ending Shingen's line. The downfall is a study in Sengoku impermanence: barely a decade after Shingen was the most feared man in Japan, his house was gone — and Nobunaga, who erased it, would himself be dead within months at Honnō-ji.

events.label: Maeda Toshiie and the great vassals
events.description: As the country reunified, trusted generals like Maeda Toshiie were rewarded with vast domains — founding the mighty daimyō houses whose descendants would still be ruling at the end of the Edo age.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Toshiie was a Nobunaga man from the start, a hot-tempered young spearman who rose through loyal service and ended up lord of Kaga — the famous 'million-koku domain,' the single richest fief in all of Japan, which his Maeda heirs held for nearly three centuries. His career captures how the unification settled out: the chaos of self-made warlords gave way to a stable aristocracy of great vassal houses planted by the victors. Trusted at the very top, Toshiie was named one of Hideyoshi's Five Elders to guard the boy Hideyori — and his death in 1599, just months after Hideyoshi's own, removed the one man whose prestige might have checked Tokugawa Ieyasu and stopped the slide to Sekigahara.

events.label: Hideyori and the seeds of the next war
events.description: Hideyoshi's son Toyotomi Hideyori survives Sekigahara as lord of Osaka Castle — a living rallying point for anti-Tokugawa loyalists, and the one loose end Ieyasu would not tie off until 1615.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: After Sekigahara, Ieyasu let the boy live, merely shrinking him from would-be ruler of Japan to one daimyō among many — but Hideyori, growing up in his father's colossal Osaka Castle, stayed a magnet for every masterless samurai and Toyotomi loyalist who resented the new order. Ieyasu, old and methodical, manufactured a pretext (an allegedly insulting inscription on a temple bell Hideyori had cast) and besieged Osaka. In 1615 the great castle fell and burned; Hideyori and his mother died in the ruins, and the Toyotomi line was extinguished. Only then, with no rival left standing, was the Tokugawa peace truly secure — the medieval age's very last battle fought to bury its second-to-last dynasty.

events.label: The medieval age closes
events.description: With the Tokugawa shogunate founded, Japan trades a century of war for centuries of sealed-off peace — and the world of the warring samurai begins turning, almost overnight, into legend.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The peace was bought by shutting the doors. Within a few decades the Tokugawa would all but ban Christianity, expel most foreigners, forbid Japanese from leaving the country on pain of death, and squeeze nearly all foreign trade through a single tightly-watched island at Nagasaki — the policy later called sakoku, the 'closed country,' which held for over two centuries. The samurai, with no wars left to fight, slowly became bureaucrats and swordsmen-philosophers, and it was in this peaceful afterglow that the polished code of bushidō was finally written down and the warring age was remade into the romantic legend the world still pictures. The medieval age of the sword ended not with a bang but with a country locking itself shut.
